newsitem.title: USA: U.S. wages, benefits edged up in 1996.
newsitem.headline: U.S. wages, benefits edged up in 1996.

text.p: American workers' pay and benefits edged higher last year, the government said Tuesday, but the increases were well within the comfort zones of inflation-wary investors on Wall Street.
Total compensation, as measured by the Labour Department's Employment Cost Index, rose 2.9 percent last year, up from 2.7 percent in 1995, but less than the 3 percent gain of 1994.
In the fourth quarter compensation rose by 0.8 percent, the department said, up from the 0.6 percent rise in the third quarter, but less than Wall Street economists had expected.
"I don't think it's enough to really be alarming in terms of inflation," said economist Bill Chemey of John Hancock Financial Services in Boston.

The news came as a relief in financial markets as traders saw no sign of wage-driven inflation that might prompt Federal Reserve policy-makers to raise short-term interest rates in a bid to hold down prices.

Stock and bond prices jumped after the report but later fell back. The Dow Jones industrial average, which rose more than 100 points during the session, retreated on profit-taking to close down 4.61 points at 6,656.08, its fifth consecutive decline.
The 30-year Treasury rose 6/32 after surging more than 1-1/4 points earlier, lowering its yield to 6.93 percent from 6.94 percent on Monday. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
Investors have been worried by signs that a tight job market would force employers to bid up wages and benefits, possibly feeding inflation.

With the economy still growing after nearly six years of expansion and the unemployment rate below 6 percent for more than two years, economists said the rise in compensation reflected in the report was not unexpected.

"It says that we are seeing a gradual acceleration in compensation growth," said economist Richard Berner of Mellon Bank in Pittsburgh. "The ongoing question is going to be, to what extent will companies absorb that in their profit margins?"
The department noted that the 0.8 percent rise in pay and benefits in the quarter was within the 0.6 percent to 0.8 percent quarterly growth range of the past three years.

The increase in compensation during the period included a 0.8 percent rise in wages and salaries and a 0.7 percent rise in the cost of benefits, mainly health care, received by employees, the department said. Both were up from increases of 0.6 percent in the third quarter of last year.

Wages and salaries, which represent about 70 percent of the Employment Cost Index, rose 3.3 percent in the past 12 months -- the biggest gain since 1991 -- after a 2.9 percent rise in 1995. The gain kept pace with the 3.3 percent rise in consumer prices last year.
Employers' costs of workers' benefits rose 2 percent last year after a 2.3 percent gain in 1995, the department said.

Benefit cost increases slowed late in 1995 and were flat in the first quarter of 1996 as employers shifted more health care costs onto their workers and turned to cheaper managed care plans. Although there has been a pick-up, benefit cost growth remains slower than wage and salary growth.

"What one sees is a creeping inflation," said economist Allen Sinai of Primark Decision Economics Inc. of Boston. "Benefits continue to hold down the overall compensation figures and the question is, how long can that go on?"

Sinai predicted workers' compensation gains will continue to pick up in the coming year. But Hancock's Chemey said gains would be modest, in part because employers have learned to avoid runaway increases in benefit costs.
"It's become a corporate priority across the country," said Chemey. "I don't think there's any way there is going to be the sort of free-wheeling increases we had in the '80s."
Small businesses, however, have been raising compensation widely in recent months, said economist Cliff Waldman of the National Federation of Independent Businesses.
In a survey of some of the federation's 600,000 members, the percentage of those who raised pay or benefits last month rose to a record, he said.
"We are definitely showing that labour market tightness is being reflected in higher compensation," said Waldman.
In another sign of a strong economy, the Conference Board said the index of U.S. consumer confidence jumped to 116.8 in January from 114.2 in December.
"The rising tide of consumer optimism that was characteristic of 1996 has spilled into 1997," said Lynn Franco of the board's Consumer Research Centre.
